AbstractText.Label: INTRODUCTION
AbstractText.content: Upper extremity (UE) trauma and subsequent immobilization affects functional performance.

AbstractText.Label: PURPOSE OF THE STUDY
AbstractText.content: Determine the usefulness and feasibility of unilateral hand training (UHT) on improving functional performance in patients with UE trauma.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: Nine participants received UHT within 10 days of immobilization. Functional performance, dexterity, grip, and pinch strength were measured at initial and 4-week visits. Qualitative interviews were coded to develop themes.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: All Jebsen-Taylor hand function test subtests improved from pretest to post-test. Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand scores of all 9 participants improved. Functional performance was more impaired for participants with dominant UE injury. Four themes emerged: participants were forced to alter or avoid most daily activities, had an increased dependency on others, took longer to perform activities, and felt UHT decreased the impact of UE trauma on function.

AbstractText.Label: DISCUSSION
AbstractText.content: Functional performance was impaired for all participants. Participants believed that UHT was useful and contributed to improved function.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: This case series tracked a comprehensive intervention based on a holistic activities of daily living framework that considered the nuances of individual complexities of immobilization following hand trauma. Knowledge from this study supports an early intervention like UHT to educate clients on effective strategies to improve immediate activities of daily living functioning and potentially prevent longer term impairments.
